title: Blood flow through a narrowed artery
passage:
Researchers modeled blood flow through a coronary artery partly blocked by plaque. In the model, blood (density 1060 kg/m³) is treated as an incompressible fluid in steady flow through a horizontal vessel. Upstream of the plaque, the artery's inner radius is 2.0 mm and the mean flow speed is 0.20 m/s.

The researchers varied how far the plaque narrowed the vessel and recorded the mean flow speed at the narrowest point (Table 1).

In a second set of runs, they held the pressure drop across a short vessel segment constant and varied the segment's radius. Volume flow rate fell steeply as radius decreased, consistent with Poiseuille's law, Q = πr⁴ΔP / (8ηL). The authors note that in a living patient, small arterioles downstream of a blockage can dilate, which partly offsets the added resistance at rest.
cap: Table 1. Flow speed at the narrowest point for four degrees of narrowing.

qs.q: Compared with the upstream segment, the blood pressure at the 1.0 mm narrowing is most likely:
qs.a: Lower, because the blood moves faster there
w: Higher, because the vessel is narrower
The same, because the fluid is incompressible
Higher, because the flow speed is higher
qs.e: For horizontal flow, Bernoulli's equation says P + ½ρv² stays constant, so the faster flow at the narrowing has lower pressure.

qs.q: What is the volume flow rate in the upstream segment?
qs.a: About 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m³/s
w: About 8.0 × 10⁻⁷ m³/s
About 1.3 × 10⁻³ m³/s
About 2.5 × 10⁻³ m³/s
qs.e: Q = Av = π(2.0 × 10⁻³ m)²(0.20 m/s) = π × 4 × 10⁻⁶ × 0.20 ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m³/s. Don't forget to convert mm to m.

qs.q: At which radius in Table 1 is the flow speed 16 times its upstream value?
qs.a: 0.5 mm
w: 1.0 mm
1.4 mm
qs.e: 3.20 / 0.20 = 16. By continuity, speed ∝ 1/r², and quartering the radius (2.0 → 0.5 mm) raises speed 16-fold.

qs.q: If a downstream arteriole doubles its radius with no other change, its resistance to flow becomes:
qs.a: 1/16 of its original value
w: 1/2 of its original value
1/4 of its original value
16 times its original value
qs.e: From Poiseuille's law, resistance = 8ηL / (πr⁴), so it scales with 1/r⁴. Doubling r divides resistance by 2⁴ = 16.

title: The bicarbonate buffer in blood
passage:
Blood pH is held near 7.4 mostly by the carbonic acid–bicarbonate buffer:

CO₂(aq) + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

Because H₂CO₃ is present only in tiny amounts and is in fast equilibrium with dissolved CO₂, physiologists use an apparent pKa of 6.1 that treats dissolved CO₂ as the acid. Dissolved CO₂ (in mM) is about 0.03 × P_CO₂ (in mmHg). In normal arterial blood, P_CO₂ is 40 mmHg and [HCO₃⁻] is 24 mM, so:

pH = 6.1 + log(24 / 1.2) = 6.1 + log 20 ≈ 7.4

The enzyme carbonic anhydrase, found in red blood cells, speeds up the conversion between CO₂ and H₂CO₃. The lungs adjust P_CO₂ within minutes by changing the rate of breathing, while the kidneys adjust [HCO₃⁻] over hours to days.

qs.q: A patient hyperventilates, lowering arterial P_CO₂ to 20 mmHg while [HCO₃⁻] stays at 24 mM. What is the blood pH? (log 2 ≈ 0.3)
qs.a: About 7.7
w: About 7.1
About 7.4
About 8.4
qs.e: Dissolved CO₂ = 0.03 × 20 = 0.6 mM. pH = 6.1 + log(24/0.6) = 6.1 + log 40 = 6.1 + 1.6 = 7.7. This is respiratory alkalosis.

qs.q: What effect does carbonic anhydrase have on the buffer system?
qs.a: It helps the system reach equilibrium faster without changing the equilibrium ratio
w: It raises the apparent pKa of the buffer, so blood pH rises at equilibrium
It shifts the equilibrium toward bicarbonate, so more H⁺ is released
It removes dissolved CO₂ from the blood, so the [HCO₃⁻]/[CO₂] ratio rises
qs.e: Enzymes are catalysts: they lower activation energy for both directions equally, so K and the equilibrium position are unchanged.

qs.q: A patient with chronic lung disease retains CO₂ for weeks. How would the kidneys most likely compensate?
qs.a: By retaining more HCO₃⁻, moving the [HCO₃⁻]/[CO₂] ratio back toward 20
w: By excreting more HCO₃⁻, lowering the ratio and the pH further
By lowering P_CO₂ directly through faster filtration in the kidney
By raising the buffer's pKa so the same ratio gives a higher pH
qs.e: High P_CO₂ lowers the ratio and the pH (respiratory acidosis). Raising [HCO₃⁻] restores the ratio, bringing pH back toward 7.4.

qs.q: Buffers usually work best within 1 pH unit of their pKa, yet this buffer works well at 7.4 even though its pKa is 6.1. What best explains this?
qs.a: It is an open system, because the lungs can quickly remove or retain CO₂
w: Blood pH actually sits much closer to 6.1 than it does to 7.4
Carbonic anhydrase raises the buffer's pKa inside red blood cells
Bicarbonate is a strong base that fully neutralizes any added acid
qs.e: Because breathing continuously sets the CO₂ concentration, added acid can be blown off as CO₂ instead of piling up as H₂CO₃.

title: Finding the focal length of a lens
passage: A student uses an optical bench to study a thin glass lens. The object is a lit arrow 2.0 cm tall. For each object distance, the student moves a screen until a sharp image appears and records the image distance. When no image can be formed on the screen, she looks through the lens and uses parallax to find where a virtual image sits. In Table 1, a negative image distance means the image is on the same side of the lens as the object.
cap: Table 1. Object and image distances for the lens.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, what kind of lens is this, and what is its focal length?
qs.a: Converging, with f = +10 cm
w: Converging, with f = +20 cm
Diverging, with f = −10 cm
Diverging, with f = −20 cm
qs.e: Any row works: 1/f = 1/20 + 1/20 = 1/10, so f = 10 cm. A positive f and real images mean a converging lens.

qs.q: When the object is 15 cm from the lens, the image is:
qs.a: 4.0 cm tall and inverted
w: 1.0 cm tall and inverted
4.0 cm tall and upright
2.0 cm tall and upright
qs.e: m = −dᵢ/dₒ = −30/15 = −2. The image is twice the 2.0 cm height (4.0 cm), and the negative sign means it is inverted.

qs.q: When the object is 5 cm from the lens, the image is:
qs.a: Virtual, upright and twice the object's size
w: Real, inverted and twice the object's size
Virtual, inverted and half the object's size
Real, upright and the same size
qs.e: dᵢ = −10 cm, so m = −(−10)/5 = +2. This is how a magnifying glass works: an object inside the focal length gives an enlarged virtual image.

qs.q: If the student places the object exactly 10 cm from the lens, what will she observe?
qs.a: No image forms, because the refracted rays leave parallel
w: A real, inverted image forms 10 cm behind the lens
A virtual, upright image forms 10 cm in front of the lens
A real image forms that is the same size as the object
qs.e: With dₒ = f, 1/dᵢ = 1/f − 1/dₒ = 0, so the image is at infinity.

title: Separating a three-part mixture
passage:
A student is given a mixture of three compounds dissolved in diethyl ether (density 0.71 g/mL): benzoic acid (pKa 4.2), aniline (pKa of its conjugate acid, the anilinium ion, is 4.6) and naphthalene (neutral, nonpolar).

Step 1: The ether solution is shaken with 1 M HCl in a separatory funnel. The aqueous layer is drained and saved as Layer A.
Step 2: The remaining ether solution is shaken with 1 M NaOH. The aqueous layer is drained and saved as Layer B.
Step 3: The ether that remains (Layer C) is dried with anhydrous MgSO₄, filtered and evaporated.

Each compound is then recovered from its own layer. Carbonic acid, formed when bicarbonate is protonated, has a pKa of about 6.4.

qs.q: Which compound is in Layer A, and in what form?
qs.a: Aniline, as the water-soluble anilinium ion
w: Benzoic acid, as the water-soluble benzoate ion
Naphthalene, unchanged and dissolved in water
Aniline, as the neutral free base in the water
qs.e: HCl protonates the basic amine, giving an ionic anilinium salt that dissolves in water. The acid and naphthalene are not protonated.

qs.q: During Step 1, where is the ether layer in the separatory funnel?
qs.a: On top, because ether is less dense than water
w: On the bottom, because ether is less dense than water
On the bottom, because it contains more solute
Mixed into the water, because both are polar
qs.e: Ether (0.71 g/mL) floats on the aqueous layer (about 1.0 g/mL). Halogenated solvents like dichloromethane sink.

qs.q: If the student used aqueous NaHCO₃ instead of NaOH in Step 2, would benzoic acid still move into the aqueous layer?
qs.a: Yes, because benzoic acid (pKa 4.2) is a stronger acid than carbonic acid (pKa 6.4)
w: No, because bicarbonate is too weak a base to deprotonate any carboxylic acid
No, because sodium bicarbonate is not soluble enough in water to work
Yes, but only if the mixture is heated so that the bicarbonate decomposes
qs.e: An acid–base reaction favors the weaker acid. Bicarbonate can deprotonate any acid stronger than carbonic acid, which includes most carboxylic acids but not phenols.

qs.q: How should the student recover solid benzoic acid from Layer B?
qs.a: Add HCl until the solution is acidic, then filter off the precipitate
w: Add more NaOH until the solution is basic, then evaporate the water
Add anhydrous MgSO₄ to the solution, then filter off the solid
Boil the solution until the sodium benzoate crystallizes as the acid
qs.e: Acidifying reprotonates benzoate back to neutral benzoic acid, which is poorly soluble in cold water and precipitates.

title: Radiotracers in medical imaging
passage:
Two isotopes dominate nuclear imaging. Technetium-99m, used in many routine scans, has a half-life of 6.0 hours. It drops from a long-lived excited nuclear state to a lower-energy state by emitting a gamma ray of about 140 keV, which a gamma camera outside the body detects.

Fluorine-18 (Z = 9), used in positron emission tomography (PET), has a half-life of about 110 minutes. It decays by positron emission. Each positron travels at most a few millimeters in tissue before meeting an electron. The two particles annihilate, producing two photons of 511 keV each that travel in nearly opposite directions. A ring of detectors records photon pairs that arrive at the same time, and a computer reconstructs where the decays happened.

Because fluorine-18 decays relatively quickly, it must be produced in a cyclotron near the imaging center.

qs.q: A dose of technetium-99m is prepared at 6 a.m. What fraction of its original activity remains at 6 a.m. the next day?
qs.e: 24 hours is 4 half-lives of 6 hours: (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.

qs.q: Fluorine-18 decays to which nucleus?
qs.a: Oxygen-18
w: Neon-18
Fluorine-17
Nitrogen-14
qs.e: Positron emission turns a proton into a neutron: Z drops from 9 to 8 (oxygen), and the mass number stays 18.

qs.q: Why do the two annihilation photons travel in nearly opposite directions?
qs.a: The total momentum was nearly zero before annihilation, and it is conserved
w: The photons carry opposite charges, so they repel each other
Total kinetic energy must be conserved, so they split it evenly
The magnetic field of the detector ring bends their paths apart
qs.e: The positron and electron are nearly at rest when they annihilate. Two photons with equal and opposite momenta keep the total near zero. Photons carry no charge.

qs.q: The energy of each annihilation photon, 511 keV, is equal to:
qs.a: The rest-mass energy of one electron
w: The binding energy of the fluorine-18 nucleus
The kinetic energy of the positron
The energy of the technetium-99m gamma ray
qs.e: E = mc² for an electron (or positron) is 511 keV. Two particles' worth of rest mass becomes two 511 keV photons.

title: Measuring a rate law
passage:
A student studies the reaction A + B → C at 25 °C using the method of initial rates. In each trial, she mixes fresh solutions of A and B and measures how quickly C forms during the first few seconds, before the concentrations change noticeably.

In a follow-up experiment, she repeats every trial at 35 °C and finds that every initial rate roughly doubles.

qs.q: What is the rate law for this reaction?
qs.a: Rate = k[A]²[B]
w: Rate = k[A][B]
Rate = k[A][B]²
Rate = k[A]²[B]²
qs.e: Trials 1 → 2: doubling [A] quadruples the rate, so it's second order in A. Trials 1 → 3: doubling [B] doubles the rate, so it's first order in B.

qs.q: What is the value of the rate constant k at 25 °C?
qs.a: 2.0 M⁻²·s⁻¹
w: 20 M⁻²·s⁻¹
qs.e: From trial 1: k = rate / ([A]²[B]) = 2.0 × 10⁻³ / (0.01 × 0.10) = 2.0 M⁻²·s⁻¹. The overall order is 3, which gives the units.

qs.q: What initial rate should the student expect for trial 4?
qs.e: Compared with trial 2, only [B] doubles, and the reaction is first order in B: 2 × 8.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.6 × 10⁻² M/s.

qs.q: What best explains why the rates double at 35 °C?
qs.a: More collisions have enough energy to get over the activation barrier
w: The activation energy of the reaction drops as the temperature rises
The reaction becomes more exothermic, which speeds up product formation
The concentrations of A and B rise because the solution expands
qs.e: By the Arrhenius equation, k = Ae^(−Ea/RT). Raising T increases k even though Ea stays the same, because more molecules have energy above Ea.
